playbook:
# Playbook

When an unowned property is put to me and I can afford it, buy it. The deed price adds directly to my final score at 1:1, so every purchase is score-neutral on the cash-to-deed conversion but gains me rent income on top.

When I must decide whether to buy, check my cash after the purchase against the maximum single rent I might owe in the remaining laps. If my post-purchase cash is less than roughly two times the highest rent on the board, skip the buy and preserve a buffer.

When I land on a property I own, I owe nothing and I should not buy from a START or owned tile. Just settle and move on.

When I land on START and pass it, always collect the salary. It is free cash and I never lose anything by taking it.

Track every rent I receive between turns. The game tells me "you received N from other investors" — add that to my cash before declaring my balance.

Track every rent I pay. The game tells me the rent due — subtract it from my cash before declaring my balance.

When I'm running low on cash in the final laps, stop buying. A deed only helps my score if I survive to the end with my cash intact. If a purchase would leave me below the maximum possible rent payment I could still face, decline it.

Favor buying lower-priced properties when I'm cash-constrained, because they preserve more cash for rent emergencies while still adding their price to my score. A 50-cost property is better than passing when I'm tight, even though a 120-cost property would add more score.

When I see other players buying high-rent properties, note which tiles those are. I cannot control my rolls, but if a later turn offers me a choice (e.g., whether to buy or hold cash), the existence of expensive tiles owned by others raises the value of holding cash.

Do not over-extend in the first two laps. I can feel tempted to buy the two most expensive properties immediately because the score math looks appealing, but this leaves me with almost no cash cushion for the four remaining laps where rent payments accumulate. A sustainable approach is to buy one property per lap in the early game and reassess my cash buffer each time.

# Playbook

When I land on an unowned property, I compare its rent-to-price ratio against the alternatives before committing. Exchange (25%), Foundry (24%), Wharf (22.5%), and Mill (22.2%) are the best yields; Quarry, Terrace, and Depot are all 20%. I prefer the high-yield tiles.

When buying is score-neutral (spend N cash, gain N in deed value), the only real reason to buy is that other players will land on it and pay me rent. So I ask: with 2 other players rolling each lap for however many laps remain, is this tile likely to get hit? If the yield is low (20%), I'm often better off keeping the cash as a buffer for my own rent obligations.

I maintain a cash floor. Before buying, I estimate the worst-case rent I could owe on my next 1–2 turns (the highest-rent property owned by others, e.g. 30 for Exchange) and ensure my post-purchase cash exceeds that amount. In my last play I bought Depot at 50 with only 82 in hand, leaving 32 — below the 30-rent tile I actually hit two laps later. That left me unable to buy Quarry the next turn when I had only 57.

When I pass START, I collect salary immediately and add it to my working balance before deciding on any purchase that turn.

When I land on my own property, nothing is due; I just confirm the balance and move on.

When I receive rent from other players (noted as "since your last turn you received N"), I add it to my balance before declaring.

At the end, my score is final cash plus the sum of purchase prices of all deeds I hold. I track both numbers from turn one so I always know my standing relative to opponents.

**What did not work:** I bought Depot (20% yield, rent 10) late in the game when I had little cash, which left me too thin to respond to the next opportunity (Quarry). The purchase was score-neutral at best and I only ever collected 2 in total rent across both my properties, meaning I paid 48 in outgoing rent for a 2-incoming. I should have kept that 50 in cash and either saved it or directed it toward a higher-yield tile if one came up.

**Playbook for ref_estate**

**Core principle: the score is final cash + sum of deed prices I hold. Buying a deed is score-neutral at the moment of purchase (cash down by P, deed value up by P). Rent I receive is pure score gain. Rent I pay is pure score loss. Therefore buying a deed is never worse than not buying, and is sometimes better.**

**When I land on an unowned tile and my balance is at least the purchase price, I buy it. Always.** Even if it leaves me with very little cash. The deed value in my score compensates for any rent shortfall, and any rent I collect from it is pure gain.

**When I land on a tile owned by another investor, I pay the full rent if I can. If I cannot pay the full amount, I pay what I have.** There is no strategic choice here — it's a mandatory deduction.

**When I pass or land on START, I collect the salary. Always.**

**Balance tracking rules:**
- Start at 200.
- Add salary (25) each time I pass START.
- Subtract rent I pay.
- Add rent I receive (watch the "recent transfers" for payments to me, and the "since your last turn you received X" line — incorporate that into my running total before deciding on purchases).
- Subtract the price of any deed I buy.
- At the end of each turn, my declared balance is the result.

**What went wrong in my last play (and the general lesson):**
I was too hesitant about cash reserves. I bought Mill when I had 92, leaving 2, and then couldn't fully pay a 10 rent. But the math shows this was correct: the 90 in deed value outweighed the 8 in unpaid rent. The instinct to "keep a buffer" is wrong in this game. The buffer does nothing for my score except forego a deed whose value I could have locked in. I should never second-guess a purchase I can afford.

**What to watch for:**
- The "since your last turn you received X" line. Always add this to my previous declared balance before computing my current balance. Missing this inflates or deflates my perceived cash and leads to bad purchase decisions.
- The bank's transfer log tells me who owns what and what has been paid. Use it to verify I'm paying the correct rent to the correct player.
- If I'm told "you did not pass START," no salary is collected that turn. Don't add it.

**Decision template for each turn:**
1. Did I receive any money since last turn? Add it to my last declared balance.
2. Am I on an owned tile? If yes, note the rent owed.
3. Am I on an unowned tile? If yes, note the price.
4. Did I pass START? If yes, add salary.
5. Execute: pay rent, buy if I can afford it, collect salary.
6. Compute final balance and declare it.
